sm: On Thanksgiving, two lucky turkeys are spared and will head to Texas to live out their days in peace. Georgia Howe and John Bickley speak with Leslie Oden, president and CEO of the National Turkey Federation, who takes part in the pardoning every year. She explains that her group helps facilitate the presentation of the turkeys to the White House, and that this year's turkeys were selected by the federation's chairwoman, Christy Puffenbarger of Avogen Turkeys. The tradition began in 1947 with President Harry Truman and has spanned fifteen administrations, making this the 79th trip to the White House. It became known as a pardon under President George H.W. Bush in the early 90s. Oden notes that Americans will still eat over 30 million turkeys on Thanksgiving, and the event puts turkey farmers and processors on a global stage.

Oden describes how this year's presidential flock was grown in West Virginia by Scott and Becky Wright. Becky is a sixth grade teacher, so local schoolchildren submitted names, the president and first lady chose among them, and the public voted. The turkeys were raised like commercial birds but were petted daily and exposed to music, pom-poms, flashing lights and visiting kids, so they would be calm around the president. They were driven to Washington, greeted with a red carpet at the Willard Intercontinental Hotel, given a suite with snacks, and shown to the media the day before the White House event. Afterward they will be flown to Texas A&M University, where the poultry science department will care for them with full-time veterinary care and nutritionists, and they will serve as ambassadors for the turkey industry. Each year a different land grant university is chosen to highlight agricultural education. Oden, a Texas A&M poultry science graduate, says Secretary Brooke Rollins suggested the school. She has worked at the federation for 17 years and calls this her 16th visit to the White House, which she describes as an honor.
sg: Raising and Retiring the Presidential Turkeys
